doc.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Bill Evans duo records; advice on guitar and piano
summary: Listening and reacting, and why duets of two chordal instruments work.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So the duo albums that were so noted just came out of that first interaction and…?

No, I told him… Yeah, I think so. And we just seemed to, to work well together and… Again, listening, listening carefully and reacting, and he, he was really fantastic at that. And, and you can hear it on the records, you know. That really doesn’t need any drums and bass fiddle and everything so… That was great. That was really a pleasure working with Bill.
Is there something specific, if you were going to talk maybe to some young people today who might, say a guitarist and a piano player…
These kids today. And were going to attempt that, and they said to you, “Well, how do you deal with it when you have two instruments that both have chordal capabilities…
What should we do? What should we think about?

Well, I assume part of it is listen to the whole texture of what’s happening and try not to, to mess it up, but to stick with the, the thing as a texture. I think I did a CD called Textures. And, and that’s a… two components of it would be… And it’s a little dicey because they tend to be in the same register a lot of the time, so you really have to listen to the other person, respect and then react. Something else I was gonna say about that. Yeah, it’s funny. People ask me about those records a lot. Yeah, I really admired Bill, and he had a great sense of humor, as well. He would do some very funny things sometimes.
